There are many good reasons :-) Here were some of mine:

1. When I visited Rice, my Dad asked one of the students something like "I hear all schools these days have grade inflation. Is that true at Rice?" And the response from random student working at the library was "Rice sets a high bar, but everyone helps each other get over that bar." This was so true in my experience -- my classes in ECE were challenging, collaborative and rewarding.

2. Ability to find mentors through the college system. I am now at a large state school, for grad school and I cannot believe how lucky I was to be to count top professors as my confidants and (dare I say) friends in college. Rice has the college system which means each student belongs to a "house" with specific masters (who are professors), RAs (who are affiliated with the university, but are not professors), and associates (again -- professors and university affiliates) who participate in college events. When I was making important life decisions, I was able to talk directly with professors who I had a strong relationship with.

3. Ability to find mentors through small classes. I was an engineering student. After my freshman classes, all professors knew my name (and the names of my peers). In grad school, my classes are bigger than the classes I had at Rice.

4. Quirky, social, interesting people. During my visit day, I found that all the people I spoke with were people I would want to be friends with. When I went to Rice I was not disappointed. Because of the college system, I am good friends with people with a variety of majors and interests. Not true for some of my friends who went to larger state schools.

5. Easy to do research. Again, speaking from an ECE perspective. It just took a few emails my sophomore year, and I was able to start working in a lab on science I thought was really cool! When I wanted to try something different my senior year, again, it just took a few quick emails.

6. Houston. I live in a perhaps more "desirable" location now, but Rice tries to bring out the cool in Houston. They frequently have free passes to the opera, ballet and symphony which I took advantage of and sorely miss :( There are also lots of great restaurants, lots of bands come through, and Houston is a drive away from some of the more "fun" TX cities (e.g., Austin). Also, Houston is hell in August/September, but October through mid April, the weather is usually quite nice, so don't let the heat scare you ;)

7. If you are interested in medicine, Rice (from what I know from having pre-med friends) is a great place to be. Rice consistently gets students into top med programs, and since it is across from the largest med center in the world, there are lots of opportunities to get involved.

8. Finally, Rice is a top university and you will get a great education there. I found the courses challenging, but I found that the professors really cared that I learned.

I could go on and on... Rice was a truly fabulous place for me to grow and learn. If you attend there, I hope you find the same. If not, I hope you find the same somewhere else.

Computer science is concerned with the study of computers and computing, focusing on algorithms, programs and programming, and computational systems. The main goal of the discipline is to build a systematic body of knowledge, theories, and models that explain the properties of computational systems and to show how this body of knowledge can be used to produce solutions to real-world computational problems.

Computer science is the intellectual discipline underlying information technology, which is widely accepted now as the ascendant technology of the next century. Students in computer science at Rice benefit from the latest in equipment and ideas as well as the flexibility of the educational programs. The research interests of the faculty include algorithms and complexity, artificial intelligence and robotics, compilers, distributed and parallel computation, graphics and visualization, computer vision and pattern recognition, natural language processing, machine learning, and artificial intelligence, operating systems, and programming languages.

The department offers two undergraduate degrees: the Bachelor of Arts (BA) degree and the Bachelor of Science in Computer Science (BSCS) degree. It also houses and oversees the Bachelor of Science (BS) degree with a major in Artificial Intelligence.

At the graduate level, the department offers a PhD degree as well as two master’s degrees: the professional Master of Computer Science (MCS) degree, the professional Master of Data Science (MDS) degree, and the research-oriented Master of Science (MS) degree. 

The MCS and MDS degrees are professional degrees for students intending to pursue a technical career. Both have an on-premise and a fully online option. Students are admitted directly into one or the other option and cannot switch between the two, but the resulting degree is the same.
The MS degree is a research degree requiring a thesis in addition to coursework. The MS degree is primarily for students pursuing their PhD. Typically, students are not admitted directly to the MS program. Students wishing to pursue a terminal master's degree should apply to the MCS program.
Students wishing to pursue a PhD should apply directly to the PhD program.

Still, it’s all worthwhile.

What is the purpose of receiving an education?

Up until about a decade ago, education was the primary facilitator of social mobility. The American Dream wasn’t just about buying a house with a white picket fence, driving a Ford, and owning the newest appliances. It was about achieving those things no matter where you came from—if you were from a rich family, a poor family, an immigrant family, or if you were an orphan. Because, back then, getting a good education was a ticket into the middle class.

Education was an accomplishment in itself—but more than that, it was a means to moving up in the world.

But in the late 90s and certainly in the 2000s, the role education played in social mobility began to change—and by the 2010s, the idea of going to college had gone from being an accomplishment to a baseline expectation. More interestingly, data showed for the first time that more education didn’t lead to more social mobility. In fact, according to Pew Research Center, “Today’s young adults are much better educated than their grandparents. Among Millennials, around 4 in 10 (39%) of those ages 25 to 37 have a bachelor’s degree or higher, compared with just 15% of the Silent Generation, roughly a quarter of Baby Boomers, and 3 in 10 Gen-Xers (29%) when they were the same age.”

In addition, “The share of young adults ages 18 to 24 currently employed (54%) has been at its lowest since the government began collecting employment data in 1948.” A study in 2010 by Pew Research Center showed that “the gap in employment between the young and all working-age adults is the widest in recorded history.”

All of this is to say: the advancement of education for the sake of one’s own intellectual curiosity is fine. But the idea that continued education will lead to better job opportunities, a higher paying salary, and more social mobility, simply isn’t true anymore.

And since, for the overwhelming majority of people, school is not for their own pursuit of knowledge but seen as a means to an end, decisions pertaining to higher education should be made accordingly—and intelligently.

School is an investment—and should be treated like one.

As of 2019, 69% of college students had taken out student loans, graduating with an average debt amount of $29,900.

The choice to attend graduate school thereafter is essentially the decision to double-down on the same loss-making investment. Like a gambler chasing a loss, your actions are saying: “I’ve made an investment. It’s not working out the way I had hoped. The returns aren’t what I expected. But I’m going to double-down and buy more.”

This is the precise moment debt begins to compound.

What began as an investment in one’s future with the hopes of increasing their social standing, suddenly becomes a slippery slope of high interest rates, delayed payments, and in today’s economy, the unfortunate realization that the job you ended up with didn’t require you to go to graduate school at all.

Of course, if you are an intellectual purist who truly believes in educational attainment for its own sake, that’s fine. However, the idea that everyone pursuing higher education ought to be doing so for no reason other than academic exploration is simply out of touch—and deeply elitist.

So, if your goal is to move up in the world, what should you do instead?

1. Let go of the outdated version of The American Dream.

The job market today is not the same job market that existed thirty years ago.

The reason the United States economy hasn’t yet moved up the value chain is because there is still the same general demand for jobs in manufacturing, retail, hospitality, etc. Yet, there’s an increased supply of “qualified candidates”—people with undergraduate and graduate degrees. With a surplus of supply, this causes droves of people to leave college only to end up unemployed or underemployed (i.e. working in jobs they could have gotten without a degree).

The mistake people make is thinking they need to double-down on their investment in order to rationalize the sunken cost of their undergraduate degree. For example, they pursue their MBA or PhD as a means to work at a company like Google, only to graduate and realize there are dramatically more candidates with comparable skills and credentials than there are vacant positions. And in the end, they settle for a general sales job that could have been obtained simply by being resourceful.

Formal education is not the only path up in society anymore.

2. Be conscious about what you’re choosing to do and why.

People want to earn a nice living, yet they end up making decisions based on status (or their perceptions thereof).

An English major may decide to pursue a graduate degree because they believe their best path forward would be to work as a writer for The New York Times. Status, and the idea of working for a prestigious publishing company, is what is driving their decision—their increased investment in formal education and their increased debt.

This is fine if you love what you’re studying and are hell-bent on working for The New York Times, but if your true goal is to just earn a living for yourself through writing, there are dozens of other options that do not require you to take on a lifetime of debt. You could hone your copywriting skills and join a high-growth startup. You could become a freelance writer and journalist for a handful of online publications—not just The New York Times. You could even apply your talents to other neglected industry segments and carve out a niche for yourself that doesn’t exist yet.

None of these options are dependent upon you pursuing a graduate degree.

Being conscious, and brutally honest about why you are pursuing higher education, is crucial to performing a risk/benefit analysis. It’s important to understand whether you are pursuing a graduate degree because your parents think you should, or because you believe this is the only path to “success.”

3. Go where the demand is—not where the approval is.

The world is one big economy, and economies reward people and businesses who “supply” the demand.

I traveled to both Ukraine and Egypt in 2018, and I learned that a college graduate in the city of Kyiv makes approximately 500 euros a month. But a college graduate who was bilingual in Russian and Chinese could make eight times that. Why? Because for that particular skill, demand vastly exceeds supply.

I witnessed the same thing in Cairo. I hired someone to be my driver while I was there, and he told me the average salary for a driver in Cairo was $300 per month. But previously, he had worked for a Japanese company whose general manager needed a driver, and he made $3,000 per month—ten times more—simply because he could also speak both Arabic and Japanese.

The skills that are most valuable today are not the ones being churned out by large academic institutions. In fact, we could make the argument that if you are being taught and trained the same way as tens of thousands of other people, you are pigeon-holing yourself into a saturated job market before you’ve even left school.

In the digital age, and the new creator economy, all the most valuable skills happen at unlikely intersections—the vast majority of which cannot be learned in a conventional classroom.

So instead of doubling-down on your investment, taking on more debt, and signing yourself up for another 2-4 years of school, I encourage you to expand your lens. Nurture new skills on your own. And realize that the pathway to social mobility today has never been shorter, if only you can rid yourself of outdated thinking and take your education into your own hands.

There is no better word than "magical" to describe my experience as an undergrad at Rice University. Indeed, Rice often invites comparisons with Hogwarts due to its Residential Colleges (much like being sorted into Hogwarts Houses), its students who take pride in being a little different, and perhaps even its campus (complete with a dungeon-like labyrinth of steam tunnels underneath the "castle" grounds). The magic I found there, though, is much deeper.

Having grown up in the Washington DC area, I didn't know what to expect when I first visited Rice: dust, tumbleweeds, and saloons? Cowboys on horseback? I had never really been to Texas (state) before and my impressions were shaped by what I had seen in popular media. Imagine my surprise when I walked through the main entrance for the first time, canopied by beautiful live oaks, and discovered a lush, verdant campus with amazing Byzantine Architecture.


It was a 300-acre oasis right in the heart of a thriving metropolis, just down the street from many of the world's most significant companies and just across the street from the world's largest medical center. Walking distance from Houston's Museum District (Houston neighborhood) and just a few hops on the light rail from the Theater District and all the major sports arenas, there was always so much going on. And yet the hedges around Rice's borders seemed to protect it magically from the frenetic energy that surrounded it. It was a place of tranquility, a place where I could see myself reading a book under a tree in the endless green space of quads, courtyards, and grounds.

When I walked into the Computer Science building without an appointment, one of the faculty invited me into his office and chatted with me for some time about the curriculum, their goals for CS grads, and what life as a CS major would be like (more time in computer labs than reading books under trees!). I was surprised by this openness of faculty to engage with students - or even prospective students in my case - but the CS department wasn't unique. There was a friendliness about Rice that I just didn't find at any of the other schools I visited. I was hooked. After I received my acceptance letter I barely even glanced at the letters from the other schools to which I had applied.

When I arrived on campus as a freshman, I quickly realized that most of the other students had been attracted to Rice for the same reasons - it was elite but not elitist. My classmates were absolutely brilliant in all sorts of ways but everyone was modest, open, and friendly. My residential college quickly became my home away from home as we all worked hard and played hard together.

Academically, I found Rice really challenging. I double majored in computer science and electrical engineering so I was already taking a heavy work load - but then I would have been remiss not to take advantage of the amazing course offerings in the humanities, arts, and literature as well. It was a struggle to keep up with it all but I wasn't alone. Rice's achievement-oriented culture meant that many other students were also pushing the boundaries of what was reasonable. Rice let us do it, though, and we banded together to help each other out.

As I labored through my classes, became involved in student government, started some clubs, and founded my first startup (and slept very little) over the course of my undergrad career, one thing that really stuck out to me was the Rice administration's trust and empowerment of its students. We were really treated like adults. Our classes were taught by faculty, not grad students, we worked on research directly with those faculty, and even dined and socialized together through the residential colleges - some faculty even lived with us on campus (our College Masters, like a Hogwarts Head of House). Students were entrusted to enforce the honor code, which added integrity to our degrees, and numerous times major problems or policy decisions were left to student leadership to solve.

This trust and and responsibility made for a unique experiential development environment. I learned an incredible amount in my classes, of course, but my most valuable development happened outside of the classroom: relationships, leadership, teamwork, communication, organization, prioritization, and general find-a-way-to-make-something-happenness. I don't understand people like Peter Thiel (businessman) who argue for students to forego a college degree. I think they miss the point of the real value created during one's time at a university and I suspect that they didn't have a magical experience like this one.

Now that it has been 15(!) years since I matriculated as a freshman at Rice, one thing is clear. The bond that was forged between so many smart, different, honest, humble students going through a unique development experience together lasts forever. I have lived around the world and every time I meet another Rice alum there is a warm glow and an instant desire to connect that stems from this bond.

Many others could probably articulate it better (and more concisely) than I have, but I hope you can tell by now that the story of Rice is a love story for me - from falling in love with the campus during that first visit to falling in love with another student who would one day become my spouse, from developing a career in entrepreneurship that I love to being inspired by professors to devote my career to creating social - not just economic - good. So perhaps the comparisons between Rice and Hogwarts aren't that far off - after all, we learn in the Harry Potter (book series) that Love is the most powerful magic of all.

They are going to be completely different experiences. Like orders of magnitude apart. And which one is “best” is incredibly subjective.

Let’s look at UCB first. Their current stats, from By the Numbers is they have over 190 active faculty members, and in 2018 had over 3,000 undergrads in the degree program and graduated 943 in the 2017–18 year.

So. Deep breath….

Rice has under 4,000 total undergraduate population. As of October 2019, the last time I had this discussion, Rice had about 600 CS students. Rice has 38 teaching faculty. Some of them JUST teach - it’s a full time gig for them versus managing research and grad students. (see Faculty)

There are two places these numbers are going to matter.

First note just the gross size difference. Rice, in total, is only slightly larger than the CS cohort at UCB.

Second, look at the student / faculty ratio. UCB: about 16:1. Rice: also about 16:1. Surprising, no? Shouldn’t be surprised - that’s a hard limit in educational efficiency. You can’t run too much “richer” than that and have decent economic performance and you can’t run too much “leaner” and have a good outcome.

But the big difference is the number of programs. You can’t run a highly diverse set of research programs on 38 faculty (even counting the not-counted research-only faculty, it’s not a lot). There are probably a dozen very solid “programs” at Rice. There are probably closer to 60–70 at UCB.

So: as an undergrad? You’re going to get about the same sort of educational experience at either place. If you’re top-10-percent at UCB, you’ll likely have an opportunity to get involved in research projects. At Rice, that’s probably move like top-third.

The real issue is what’s the UNIVERSITY experience going to be.

Rice spends a lot of time looking not just at your academic performance, but at what you as a person bring to the campus, to campus life. The administration has various groups that spend a lot of time thinking about the experience of being a student, and how to use that experience to help you maximize being the person you can become - on your terms.

The “learning” part? You can get that anywhere. You can also get nearly all of that “nowhere” - via online resources.

But that “being” part? That’s what you need to pay attention to.

I know that I got a huge amount of value out of being on a small campus with a small cohort (my entering class was under 450), in an incredibly accelerated environment. My other choices were MIT and CalTech, the big schools weren’t even on my list.

On the other hand, I have friends who went to some of the really, really big schools. It worked for them.

By the time we all got to grad school, we’d “become”, and the undergrad portion that shaped us was ever present, but not nearly as front and center in our performance in grad school.

But I guarantee you, it’ll be front and center in a whole bunch of stuff the rest of your life.

I can give you a perspective about the department for undergraduates. I'm not sure how things are for graduate students.

In short, Rice's Computer Science department is a hidden gem.

The first year curriculum is quite different from a typical Computer Science program. It's designed to accommodate both students who began programming at an early age and those who have never programmed and want to major in Computer Science. COMP 140, COMP 182, COMP 215, and COMP 310 are all taught really well and are some of the most exhilarating courses I've taken at Rice.

The knowledge imparted through the program is very theory intensive, and despite that you get a lot of programming practice through rigorous assignments. This leads to a ridiculous number of hours spent on the assignments and they begin to get extremely difficult towards the end of the semester. However, help is always there for those who seek it.

Because of this rigor and strong theoretical foundation, CS graduates from Rice are great at picking up new knowledge and can rapidly learn new technologies and have a good sense of design in software engineering.

Despite all of this, most of my colleagues and I have managed to have a very decent social life. Though there were times when I felt as if I barely slept.

A good portion of our students work at top companies such as Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Facebook, etc.



Let me start with a story.

When I worked for Rice IT, one of the other student workers at the Help Desk, a TA for Algorithmic Thinking, was grading assignments aloud during down time. He mused, "The same mistake?" after marking down a few papers in a row for a less than optimal run time. Seconds later, "What the fuck! They implemented it straight from the library." In other words, code from libraries are already the fastest and most concise. He cursed, furiously bringing up the mistaken grading sheet.

Only, as it happens, Prof. Rixner came up with his own implementation, more elegant than the publicly-sourced, official Python Library version. NBD.

Rice had a major hit on Coursera this year in Intro to Interactive Programming with Python, one of our CS Intro classes. The shine that drew people, I think, was the learn-by-building-games approach and that Prof. Rixner built a Python IDE right into the browser (CodeSkulptor). If you've ever taken programming, you know the pains of setting up an IDE as a beginner.

If you take the class at Rice, you'll pitch and design a game in the second half. This is a rare class where you'll leave with something to show, some creative output; I promise it will be a long time before you build something of your own in Physics or Math. A lot of my classmates left with pretty awesome arcade games, first semester of freshman year.

That said, we don't have hotshot professors here. No Turing Awards at office hours. You won't read "truly remarkable things being done for the field" in the Times. And there certainly are departments in this country where every single professor there has some small claim to this hotshottedness. You won't miss out on creative output either (Berkeley's SaaS course assigns teams to build for non-profit groups, for instance; MIT's toy lab too). Cal has three EECS buildings; we kinda have a collection of hallways in Duncan Hall. Stanford has the Gates Computer Science Building; we don't even have a CS lounge. We have fewer CS clubs and teams, and a lot fewer awards.

Maybe you'll come to Rice because the world is big and life is short. But don't come just because you're attracted to a vision of smaller class sizes and approachable professors. Rice CS just redid its entire undergrad curriculum. It may very well someday be strong, and I am sure the professors have desire for good teaching in their hearts. Rice is throwing itself into the new MOOC culture, and if you matriculate in the near future, there's a good chance of professors piloting Coursera and EdX course's on you.

If Rice is one of your choices because you're afraid you wouldn't get to work with the professors at the big, bad schools anyway, let me tell you this. You are good enough. You can go. And excel. And catch the attention of that professor you want to work with.

And if it so happens they won't take you and Rice does, or if you're already here, you'll know that, in every way that matters, you're not settling for less.

P.S. CS, and every department at Rice, has some connection with medicine, probably because the massive Texas Medical Center next door. There is something to be said about Rice having one of the fastest supercomputers, but it's being used to study diseases at the BRC. If you're interested specifically in using CS in medicine, Rice's position, I think, is pretty unique.

It depends on your measure of "goodness": Do you think a department is good because it has Turing award winners or because of diversity in courses or larger/smaller student body or on-campus jobs available to undergrads/Masters/PhD or something else ? This measure also differs based on whether you are talking to a undergrad (see Waseem's answer) or doing your Masters or a graduate student (that's me), as each of them have different expectation from the department.

So as to not misrepresent Rice's student body, I will give an answer to a different question: "What is a typical PhD student's perspective of Rice University's Computer Science department ?" ... and let you infer the answer to above mentioned question :-P

- I only came to Rice University because my advisor moved here, but in hindsight I couldn't have taken a better decision :-)
- Rice admin staff and then chair were very accommodating (and still are) with the transition process and helped me a lot with waiving few of the requirements. Why am I pointing this out ? Well, in some public universities where number of enrolled students is very large, the sheer volume of paperwork/cases sometimes makes admin staff pretty unaccommodating and sometimes rude.
- Big shots ... sure, they are good for publicity, but what really matters to a graduate student is the faculty's publication record and also whether they are still publishing in top-tier journals/conferences ... Why ? We need to graduate in 5-6 years and get a job ;-) ... Btw, if you think Turing awards makes one a big shot, I suspect Moshe will get one in recent future :-)
- I agree that there are fewer clubs and the current chair (along with few enthusiastic students) is trying to address that. So, as far as graduate students are concerned, there are relatively fewer opportunities to socialize ... though friday night gatherings at on-campus student-run pub Valhalla (which serves cheap beers) does help ;-)
- Some classes are small, while others are quite big ... it depends on popularity and also type of the course (seminar oriented, coding intensive, theory intensive, introductory or advanced) ... so class size should not really be a motivating factor to chose Rice (at least not for a graduate student). That said, it is important to point out that among (very selected) courses that I took, I found the professors pretty approachable and helpful.
- Based on casual discussions with other graduate students, most of them seem pretty happy with their advisors (with issues like micro-managing, choice of problems, rapport, etc).
- Funding situation is pretty good compared to other universities. Also, offices with 3 students per room are assigned to graduate students, which helps if you need peace and quiet while working ... some may like it, others may prefer a "big" lab-like environment.
- There is lot of buzz going on in entrepreneurship at Rice for last few years. MBA-school is offering pretty good course on it, plus there are events like 3-day startup which are useful to both undergrads and grads. Rice OTT is also pretty helpful in this area.

Since Rice has smaller department, on an average, there are 2-3 professors per research area. Some research areas have just one. So, here is my suggestion for prospective graduate students: Do little bit of homework before applying here. If you are somewhat sure about which area you want to work in and if you like the publication record of the "prospective" advisor in that area, then and then only apply here. If you are totally clueless, you may either hit a gold mine and find a right advisor or you may end up settling (or changing the university).

There are many good reasons :-) Here were some of mine:

1. When I visited Rice, my Dad asked one of the students something like "I hear all schools these days have grade inflation. Is that true at Rice?" And the response from random student working at the library was "Rice sets a high bar, but everyone helps each other get over that bar." This was so true in my experience -- my classes in ECE were challenging, collaborative and rewarding.

2. Ability to find mentors through the college system. I am now at a large state school, for grad school and I cannot believe how lucky I was to be to count top professors as my confidants and (dare I say) friends in college. Rice has the college system which means each student belongs to a "house" with specific masters (who are professors), RAs (who are affiliated with the university, but are not professors), and associates (again -- professors and university affiliates) who participate in college events. When I was making important life decisions, I was able to talk directly with professors who I had a strong relationship with.

3. Ability to find mentors through small classes. I was an engineering student. After my freshman classes, all professors knew my name (and the names of my peers). In grad school, my classes are bigger than the classes I had at Rice.

4. Quirky, social, interesting people. During my visit day, I found that all the people I spoke with were people I would want to be friends with. When I went to Rice I was not disappointed. Because of the college system, I am good friends with people with a variety of majors and interests. Not true for some of my friends who went to larger state schools.

5. Easy to do research. Again, speaking from an ECE perspective. It just took a few emails my sophomore year, and I was able to start working in a lab on science I thought was really cool! When I wanted to try something different my senior year, again, it just took a few quick emails.

6. Houston. I live in a perhaps more "desirable" location now, but Rice tries to bring out the cool in Houston. They frequently have free passes to the opera, ballet and symphony which I took advantage of and sorely miss :( There are also lots of great restaurants, lots of bands come through, and Houston is a drive away from some of the more "fun" TX cities (e.g., Austin). Also, Houston is hell in August/September, but October through mid April, the weather is usually quite nice, so don't let the heat scare you ;)

7. If you are interested in medicine, Rice (from what I know from having pre-med friends) is a great place to be. Rice consistently gets students into top med programs, and since it is across from the largest med center in the world, there are lots of opportunities to get involved.

8. Finally, Rice is a top university and you will get a great education there. I found the courses challenging, but I found that the professors really cared that I learned.

I could go on and on... Rice was a truly fabulous place for me to grow and learn. If you attend there, I hope you find the same. If not, I hope you find the same somewhere else.
